newsitem.title: UK: Opening Euro markets spur telecom mergers - report.
newsitem.headline: Opening Euro markets spur telecom mergers - report.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
The prospect of open markets in Europe's telephone business in 1998 is likely to inspire a wave of mergers this year following a frenzy of acquisitions in 1996, a report published on Thursday said.
Merger and acquisitions adviser Broadview Associates said the value of deals jumped almost 50 percent last year and more of the same could be expected in 1997.
"With full deregulation around the corner in 1998, more acquisition opportunities will emerge," Broadview managing director Garry Stephen said.
"1996 was an exciting year for the telecom services sector in Europe as the now irreversible trend towards liberalisation drove the pace of transactions upward," Stephen said.
Privatisation and deregulation will gather pace this year ahead of the European Union's decree that all telephone markets will be free from government dominance on January 1, 1998.
Deutsche Telekom was partly privatised last November. The French government is expected to sell 20 percent of France Telecom in May.
The old, over-manned state-owned telephone utilities are trying to reinvent themselves as aggressive, flexible companies with shareholders and stockmarket quotes.

The business is being revolutionised by the computer. Customers not only want more, cheaper, phones -- often mobile phones -- they also want to plug their personal computers into the telephone network, and shop, bank and communicate across the Internet.

Last year, the 168 mergers and acquisitions in Europe's telecommunications services markets reached a record $30.1 billion, up almost 50 percent from 1995, according to Broadview, and compared with 98 deals worth $20.1 billion in 1995.
The pace of deals accelerated throughout the year, it said.

The telecommunications services segments which received most attention included newly formed multi-service operator groupings such as Generale des Eaux's Cegetel, in which British Telecommunications Plc bought a 25 percent stake.
The cable and wireless segments were also popular with investors, the report said.
The report's main conclusions were:

-- DEREGULATED AND EMERGING MARKETS BUSIEST. Twenty-two percent of sellers in telecom services came from Britain, the most deregulated market in Europe. Emerging markets of eastern Europe are tempting buyers willing to risk regulatory and economic uncertainty for potentially high returns.
-- NATIONAL OPERATORS, NEW PLAYERS MOST ACTIVE. Most active were Europe's state companies and new operators like Mannesmann AG, MFS Communication, Vebacom and RWE's Telliance, and U.S. operators.
Koninklijke PTT Nederland was the most aggressive with eight acquisitions, followed by US West Inc with five and Deutsche Telekom, Mannesmann, and Vodafone each with four.

-- WIRELESS AND CABLE DEALS DOUBLE. In 1996 48 wireless deals were worth $3.2 billion, up from 1995's 25 deals worth $2 billion. Cable deals rose a similar amount with value leaping to $6.2 billion from $3.5 billion, as both sectors sought greater access to customers.

-- BRITISH CABLE WILL CONSOLIDATE FURTHER. Britain is in the midst of its second cable consolidation following the $8.8 billion merger of Bell Cablemedia, Videotron, NYNEX Cable Communications Group Plc, and Cable and Wireless' Mercury.
